objectives: Master the algorithmic-society canon — Zuboff, Eubanks, Benjamin, O'Neil.
Survey platform sociology — Vaidhyanathan, van Dijck, Gillespie, Sweeney.
Address AI in sociology — synthetic populations, LLMs as research subjects, risks + future of the discipline.

slides.title: Algorithmic society: Zuboff, Eubanks, Benjamin, O'Neil
slides.body:
**Algorithmic society** = social life organized by + through algorithmic decision systems — credit scoring, predictive policing, welfare eligibility, hiring screens, content recommendation, criminal-justice risk assessment. A wave of major sociological + adjacent works in 2016-2019 turned the discipline's attention to algorithmic stratification + power; the subfield is now central.

**Shoshana Zuboff — *The Age of Surveillance Capitalism* (2019)**. Harvard Business School emerita; an 691-page synthesis that named the dominant 21st-century accumulation regime.
- **Surveillance capitalism** = a logic of accumulation in which firms extract *behavioral surplus* (data about user behavior beyond what is needed to provide a service), processed into *prediction products* sold in *behavioral futures markets*. Google + Facebook are paradigmatic.
- Continues Polanyi's *Great Transformation* (1944) — three fictitious commodities (land, labor, money); Zuboff adds a fourth: *human experience*.
- **Instrumentarian power** (distinct from Arendt's totalitarianism): rule by behavioral modification rather than terror.
- **Critiques**: monolithic; underweights non-Western capitalism + Chinese surveillance models; doesn't fully theorize the state. Influential nonetheless as a sociology-meets-political-economy synthesis.

**Virginia Eubanks — *Automating Inequality* (2018)**. Political scientist / public-policy scholar; ethnographic + investigative case studies of three algorithmic systems:
- **Coordinated Entry homeless-services system** (Los Angeles): risk-scoring homeless individuals to allocate scarce housing — sorting + denying as much as helping.
- **Indiana welfare-eligibility automation** (2006-2009): privatized + automated TANF/SNAP/Medicaid eligibility; massive denial of benefits; lawsuit + reversal.
- **Allegheny County child-welfare risk score**: predicting which families warrant investigation; concentrated surveillance on poor families.
Key thesis: the *digital poorhouse* — algorithmic systems disproportionately surveil + control poor + working-class + Black + brown people, while the affluent are governed by light-touch contracts + opt-in services. The book is the canonical ethnographic + policy-anchored account of algorithmic harm to the poor.

**Ruha Benjamin — *Race After Technology* (2019)**. Princeton sociologist + author of *Viral Justice* (2022).
- **The New Jim Code**: a riff on Michelle Alexander's *New Jim Crow* (2010) — the application of new technologies that *reflect* + *reproduce* existing inequities, often presented as more objective + progressive than the human decisions they replace.
- Four key moves: (1) *engineered inequity* — bias by design; (2) *default discrimination* — bias from defaults that fit the majority; (3) *coded exposure* — racialized risks of being miscoded (or coded at all); (4) *technological benevolence* — bias under the guise of inclusion.
- Examples: predictive policing (PredPol; ShotSpotter); name-based ad targeting (Sweeney); credit scoring; gang databases; facial recognition (Buolamwini + Gebru 2018 *Gender Shades*); voice + speech recognition.
- Methodologically: combines tech-studies, critical race theory (Crenshaw + Bell + Bonilla-Silva), feminist STS (Haraway, Subramaniam), and ethnography.

**Cathy O'Neil — *Weapons of Math Destruction* (2016)**. Mathematician-turned-data-scientist + auditor. A more popular but influential account. *WMDs* = algorithmic systems that are *opaque*, *scale*, and *damage*. Examples:
- **Teacher value-added models** (D.C. IMPACT) firing teachers based on noisy + unstable test-score growth models.
- **Recidivism risk scores** (COMPAS; Northpointe) deployed in criminal sentencing despite documented racial disparities (ProPublica's *Machine Bias* 2016 — Angwin et al. — sparked the modern algorithmic-fairness field; cross-ref Corbett-Davies + Goel 2018 on fairness criteria).
- **Credit scoring + insurance scoring** + their feedback loops.
- **Personality + employment tests** for retail + service hiring.
- **Predatory advertising** targeting the desperate.
O'Neil's analytic — opacity + scale + damage + feedback — is now standard short-hand for thinking about algorithmic harm.

**Related work**:
- **Frank Pasquale, *The Black Box Society* (2015)** — opacity + accountability.
- **Safiya Umoja Noble, *Algorithms of Oppression* (2018)** — search-engine bias against Black women.
- **Meredith Broussard, *Artificial Unintelligence* (2018) + *More Than a Glitch* (2023)**.
- **Kate Crawford, *Atlas of AI* (2021)** — AI's materiality (rare earth, labor, energy, data).
- **Joy Buolamwini, *Unmasking AI* (2023) + Algorithmic Justice League**.
- **Pasquale + Citron** on procedural due process for algorithmic decisions.
The canon insists: algorithms are *not* neutral; they are *socio-technical* systems whose biases are *engineered* (often unintentionally) into training data + objective functions + deployment contexts; sociologists have unique tools to study them.

slides.title: Platform sociology: Vaidhyanathan, van Dijck, Gillespie, Sweeney
slides.body:
**Platform sociology** treats digital platforms — Facebook / Meta, X / Twitter, YouTube / Google, Amazon, Uber, TikTok / ByteDance, Spotify, Airbnb — as the central institutions organizing 21st-century public life, commerce, labor, and culture.

**Siva Vaidhyanathan — *Anti-Social Media: How Facebook Disconnects Us and Undermines Democracy* (2018)**. UVA media-studies scholar. Argues Facebook's architecture (engagement-maximizing News Feed + ad-tech + scale + global reach) is structurally hostile to democratic deliberation. Earlier work — *The Googlization of Everything* (2011) — extends to Google. Subsequent academic conversation about platform governance + content moderation owes much to Vaidhyanathan's framing.

**José van Dijck — *The Culture of Connectivity* (2013) + *The Platform Society* (with Poell + de Waal 2018)**. University of Utrecht. The *platform society* is governed by a small number of platforms whose architectures + business models reshape public values (privacy, accuracy, ownership, accountability). Van Dijck's *Big Five* (Google, Meta, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft) + parallel Chinese platforms (Tencent, Alibaba, ByteDance, Baidu) provide the institutional substrate. Sociology of values + governance.

**Tarleton Gillespie — content moderation + platform governance**. *Custodians of the Internet* (2018, Yale). Cornell + Microsoft Research. Tracks how platforms govern speech + behavior through *content moderation* — Terms of Service, community guidelines, content policies, algorithmic ranking, human reviewers (the *moderation labor* problem: traumatized contractors in Manila + Hyderabad + the U.S., often poorly paid + unsupported). Moderation is *not* a neutral application of rules; it is *political* + *cultural* + *labored*. Subsequent work: Sarah T. Roberts *Behind the Screen* (2019), Robyn Caplan, danah boyd.

**Latanya Sweeney — algorithmic discrimination**. Harvard computer scientist + former FTC chief technologist; a foundational figure in algorithmic discrimination research.
- **Sweeney 2002**: k-anonymity + the broader re-identification critique — 87% of U.S. residents identifiable by ZIP + DOB + gender alone (cross-ref data ethics).
- **Sweeney 2013, 'Discrimination in Online Ad Delivery'** (CACM): Google search for Black-sounding names ('Latanya' itself) returned ads suggesting arrest records ~25% more often than white-sounding names — *audit-style* CSS evidence of algorithmic discrimination.
- Foundational for *algorithmic auditing* as a method (Sandvig et al. 2014; Raji + Buolamwini 2019 *Actionable Auditing*).

**Platform-labor sociology**.
- **Alex Rosenblat, *Uberland* (2018)**: ethnography of algorithmic management in ride-share work.
- **Mary L. Gray + Siddharth Suri, *Ghost Work* (2019)**: the hidden human labor (data labeling, content moderation, AI training) that powers 'autonomous' AI.
- **Antonio Casilli, *Waiting for Robots* (English 2025; French *En attendant les robots* 2019)**: digital labor + click-work.
- **Niels van Doorn + others** on the platform labor of Mechanical Turk + ScaleAI + Appen.
- **Vili Lehdonvirta, *Cloud Empires* (2022)**: platform sovereignty.

**Platform politics + content moderation debates**:
- **Sarah T. Roberts** + Gillespie + Caplan + boyd on moderation labor + governance.
- **Daphne Keller, Eric Goldman** on legal frameworks (Section 230 in the U.S.; EU Digital Services Act; UK Online Safety Act).
- **The disinformation literature** — Yochai Benkler + Robert Faris + Hal Roberts *Network Propaganda* (2018); Whitney Phillips; Joan Donovan + Brian Friedberg.
- **The Facebook Papers + 'Facebook Files'** (Wall Street Journal 2021; Frances Haugen testimony) revealed internal awareness of harms — research data subsequently restricted.
- **Bail's Polarization Lab + Guess et al. 2023 Meta election studies** (lesson 7) provide rigorous experimental evidence.

**Synthetic + dating platforms + sex + intimacy**:
- **Marie Bergström, *The New Laws of Love* (2021)** + **Bumble / Tinder / Hinge research** on algorithmic mediation of intimate life.

**The state, surveillance + the platform**:
- **Sarah Brayne, *Predict and Surveil* (2020)**: LAPD + predictive policing ethnography.
- **Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, *The Rise of Big Data Policing* (2017)**.
- **Chinese social-credit + surveillance literature** (Daithí Mac Síthigh, Karen Hao reporting, academic syntheses).

Platform sociology integrates: Bourdieusian field analysis (platforms as fields with their own doxa); Goffmanian dramaturgy (online presentation of self); Foucauldian governmentality (algorithmic regulation of conduct); Marxian political economy (labor + capital + commodification); intersectional analysis (whose data, whose harms). Each classical lens illuminates a dimension of platform life.

slides.title: AI + sociology: synthetic populations, LLMs as research subjects, risks, the discipline's future
slides.body:
The most rapidly evolving research frontier in sociology. Lesson 7 introduced LLM-augmented research; this slide extends to the broader role of AI in + as sociology, the risks involved, and the discipline's future.

**Synthetic populations + LLMs as research subjects**.
- **Argyle, Busby, Fulda, Gubler, Rytting, Wingate 2023 *Political Analysis*, 'Out of One, Many'**: prompted GPT-3 with demographic profiles matched to ANES; the model reproduced response patterns surprisingly well — but with systematic biases (over-representing some demographics, under-representing others; flattening dissent within subgroups). A landmark + a controversy.
- **Hewitt + Ashokkumar + Ghezae + Willer 2024 (CSS conferences + preprints)**: refined protocols for LLM-augmented qualitative + quantitative work; explicit attention to bias, prompt stability, replication.
- **Park + Bernstein 2023, 'Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior'**: Stanford's 25 LLM-driven NPCs in a virtual town — bottom-up generative ABM (cross-ref Epstein-Axtell Sugarscape, lesson 7) using LLMs as agents.
- **Vezhnevets et al. 2023 'Concordia'** + DeepMind frameworks for LLM-based social simulation.
- **AI-generated 'silicon samples'**: cheaper + faster than fielding surveys; useful for *pilot* + *exploratory* work + *out-of-domain extrapolation* checks; not (yet) a substitute for real survey data. The intellectual + political stakes are large.

**LLMs as objects of sociological study** (the reverse direction).
- LLMs are trained on text reflecting class + race + gender + ideological + linguistic biases of the corpora.
- **Bolukbasi 2016, Caliskan + Bryson + Narayanan 2017 *Science*, Gebru + Buolamwini *Gender Shades* 2018** (lesson 7 + 5) established embedded-bias measurement.
- **Bender + Gebru + McMillan-Major + Mitchell 2021, 'On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots'** (FAccT): foundational critique of LLM scaling — environmental + labor + bias + epistemic risks.
- **Birhane + Prabhu + Kahembwe 2021 on dataset audit**.
- **Sociology of AI hype + boosterism** — Crawford, Whittaker, Bender, Hanna, Suchman, Gebru's Distributed AI Research (DAIR).
- **Sociology of AI labor**: Gray + Suri *Ghost Work* (2019); Sandhya Sankaran + others on Mechanical Turk + reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback (RLHF) data annotation.

**Risks of AI-augmented sociology**:
- **Bias laundering**: AI tools encode biases that, when used in sociological research, are *laundered* as empirical findings unless audited (Buolamwini + Gebru; Garg 2018; cross-ref lesson 5 + lesson 7).
- **Replication + transparency**: LLM versions change; reproducibility requires explicit prompt + model + parameter documentation + (ideally) open-source models.
- **Privacy + consent + IRB**: synthetic populations + generative agents do not solve consent + privacy questions; deepfakes + synthetic data have their own ethics.
- **Concentration of compute**: only a few institutions can train frontier LLMs; the discipline risks dependence on Google / Meta / OpenAI / Anthropic infrastructure.
- **The displacement of the field worker + ethnographer**: synthetic interviewing tempts cost-cutting; lived experience cannot (yet?) be simulated; intersectional + critical traditions warn that the *Black Box Society* (Pasquale) + *Algorithms of Oppression* (Noble) reproduce harm.
- **Theoretical inflation**: when everything is 'AI', the term loses content; sociologists must be precise about which technology + which architecture + which deployment.

**The discipline's future** — open questions:
- *How does sociology study itself* as algorithmically mediated? (Wagner et al. 2021 *Nature*, 'Measuring algorithmically infused societies'.)
- *Should sociology train its own LLMs* on sociological corpora (papers, transcripts, interviews) with open access + audit-by-design?
- *How do classical concepts — class, race, gender, capital, habitus, performativity, intersectionality — apply to algorithmic + AI-mediated social life*? Hochschild's *emotional labor* in customer-service chatbots? Goffman's *front stage / back stage* on TikTok? Bourdieu's *fields* in algorithmic recommendation? Crenshaw's *intersectionality* in algorithmic-fairness criteria (Buolamwini + Gebru)? Du Bois's *double-consciousness* for racialized users navigating algorithmic systems? Mills's *sociological imagination* for understanding AI personal-troubles as public-issues?
- *What does just-transition sociology look like* as AI reshapes labor, education, intimacy, governance?
- *Who counts as a sociologist + a knower* in the age of synthetic populations + computational + LLM-augmented research?

**Closing synthesis**. Sociology started as a 19th-century response to industrialization (Comte, Marx, Engels, Durkheim, Weber). It now responds to *algorithmic + AI capitalism* — Zuboff's surveillance capitalism, Eubanks's digital poorhouse, Benjamin's New Jim Code, O'Neil's WMDs, Vaidhyanathan + van Dijck + Gillespie + Sweeney on platforms, the LLM revolution from Argyle to Hewitt. The classical canon is more relevant than ever; it requires translation + extension. The discipline's future lies in the integration of classical theory, rigorous causal + computational methods, ethnographic + intersectional attention to lived experience, and rigorous + ethical engagement with the AI tools that are now *both* its instruments + its objects of study.

Welcome to 21st-century sociology.

question.question: Apply the algorithmic-society canon to a real case
question.goal: A U.S. county adopts a child-welfare predictive-risk score to triage abuse + neglect reports. Diagnose with Zuboff + Eubanks + Benjamin + O'Neil + Sweeney.

steps.prompt: What is the system + what is its stated purpose?

acceptedAnswers: an algorithmic risk score predicts which reported children are at highest risk of harm to prioritize investigation

steps.reveal: A statistical / ML system ingests historical administrative data (prior CPS contact, parental criminal record, family demographics, public-benefits use, ZIP) + outputs a risk score for each new report. Higher-score cases are prioritized for in-person investigation. Stated purpose: improve resource allocation + child safety + (sometimes) reduce *bias* in triage relative to caseworker judgment. Allegheny County (PA) is the canonical published case; Eubanks's *Automating Inequality* (2018) documents it in depth.

steps.prompt: What does Eubanks's *digital poorhouse* analysis predict?

acceptedAnswers: the system disproportionately surveils + flags + intervenes in poor + Black + brown families

hints: Whose data is in the training set + who gets flagged?
steps.reveal: The training data — historical CPS contacts, public-benefits use, prior criminal-justice contact — is itself a record of *who has been surveilled* + *who has been poor*. Affluent families with private pediatricians, attorneys, + private mental-health care leave no comparable trace. Eubanks's *digital poorhouse* prediction: the algorithm encodes the existing surveillance asymmetry + outputs higher risk for poor + Black + brown families, then deploys the very state attention that generates the *next* round of training data. A feedback loop reproducing structural inequality.

steps.prompt: How does Benjamin's *New Jim Code* + Buolamwini-Gebru-style audit deepen the critique?
steps.motivation: Race + bias in the technical system.

acceptedAnswers: the system is presented as more objective but encodes historical racial bias; subgroup audit reveals disparate error rates

hints: Engineered inequity + default discrimination + technological benevolence.
steps.reveal: Benjamin's *New Jim Code*: the system is sold as *more objective* + *less biased* than caseworker judgment, but inherits + scales the racism of the data + the institution. Subgroup audit (à la Buolamwini + Gebru *Gender Shades* 2018) is essential — false-positive + false-negative rates by race + class + neighborhood — and almost always reveals disparities. *Engineered inequity* (bias by design choices about training data + features); *default discrimination* (defaults that fit the majority); *technological benevolence* (bias presented as protection).

acceptedAnswers: subgroup audit, transparency, due process, community oversight, sociological + ethnographic study, moratorium where appropriate

hints: Audit + transparency + governance + the option to not deploy.
steps.reveal: Responses: (1) *Subgroup audit* + public reporting of error rates by race + class + ZIP (cross-ref Buolamwini + Raji 2019 Actionable Auditing); (2) *Procedural due process* (Citron + Pasquale 2014) — affected families' rights to explanation, contest, appeal; (3) *Community oversight + impact assessments* (Algorithmic Accountability Act proposals); (4) *Sociological + ethnographic study* of deployment effects, à la Eubanks + Brayne *Predict and Surveil* (2020) + Benjamin; (5) *Moratorium + abolition* where harm exceeds benefit + remediation is infeasible (cf. facial recognition bans in some U.S. cities; AI Now + Stop LAPD Spying Coalition advocacy). The classical sociological + intersectional toolkit + algorithmic-audit toolkit + EJ-style community organizing must be deployed together.

question.question: Why has Ruha Benjamin's *Race After Technology* (2019) become canonical in the algorithmic-society literature?
options: Benjamin (Princeton) crystallized the *New Jim Code* — a riff on Michelle Alexander's *New Jim Crow* (2010) — to name how new technologies *reflect* + *reproduce* existing racial inequities while being presented as more objective + progressive than the human decisions they replace. Four key moves — *engineered inequity*, *default discrimination*, *coded exposure*, *technological benevolence* — give analysts a sharp vocabulary. The book synthesizes critical race theory (Crenshaw, Bell, Bonilla-Silva — lesson 5), feminist STS, ethnography, and tech studies, with vivid cases — predictive policing, name-based ad targeting (Sweeney 2013), credit scoring, gang databases, facial recognition (Buolamwini + Gebru 2018 *Gender Shades*), voice recognition. Paired with Eubanks's *digital poorhouse* (2018), O'Neil's WMDs (2016), Zuboff's surveillance capitalism (2019), Noble's *Algorithms of Oppression* (2018), and Pasquale's *Black Box Society* (2015), it founded the contemporary sociology + tech-studies engagement with algorithmic + AI-mediated inequality.
question.explanation: Benjamin's *Race After Technology* (2019) coined the *New Jim Code* (riffing on Alexander's *New Jim Crow* 2010) — engineered inequity + default discrimination + coded exposure + technological benevolence. Synthesized CRT + feminist STS + ethnography. Paired with Eubanks 2018, O'Neil 2016, Zuboff 2019, Noble 2018, Pasquale 2015, it founded contemporary sociology of algorithmic + AI inequality.

hints: Why is it paradigm-shaping for sociology of tech?
slides.workedSolution: Benjamin's *Race After Technology* (2019) named the *New Jim Code* — engineered inequity + default discrimination + coded exposure + technological benevolence — for how new tech reflects + reproduces racial inequity. Synthesized CRT + feminist STS + ethnography. With Eubanks 2018, O'Neil 2016, Zuboff 2019, Noble 2018, Pasquale 2015 it founded sociology of algorithmic + AI inequality.

question.question: The sociology department + the frontier
question.prompt: Your sociology department is debating a 5-year strategic plan. A faction proposes hiring three FTEs specifically for AI + algorithmic-society research (covering algorithmic audit + LLM-augmented methods + platform governance + critical AI studies). Another faction worries this will displace ethnography + critical race / gender / intersectional work + classical theory. Drawing on (a) the Lazer CSS manifestos (lesson 7) + Argyle + Hewitt frontier; (b) Zuboff + Eubanks + Benjamin + O'Neil + Vaidhyanathan + van Dijck + Gillespie + Sweeney from this lesson; and (c) the intersectionality + race / class / gender literatures (lessons 5 + 6), write a ≤220-word memo proposing a *both / and* strategy. Identify three specific course or hire categories that integrate algorithmic + classical sociology rather than substituting one for the other.

question.question: An algorithmic-audit study finds a facial-recognition system with overall accuracy 92%, but subgroup accuracy is 99% for light-skinned men and 65% for dark-skinned women (cf. Buolamwini + Gebru 2018 *Gender Shades*). Compute the accuracy gap $\Delta = 0.99 - 0.65$ between these two subgroups, as a decimal.
question.hint: $0.99 - 0.65 = 0.34$. Buolamwini + Gebru's *Gender Shades* (2018) revealed 34-point accuracy gaps in commercial facial recognition (IBM, Microsoft, Face++) — a foundational algorithmic audit demonstrating disparate error rates by race + gender + their intersection. Inspired the IBM + Microsoft retractions + the algorithmic-fairness field.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, articulate the modern frontier of sociology by (a) naming one algorithmic-society work + concept (Zuboff, Eubanks, Benjamin, or O'Neil), (b) one platform-sociology work (Vaidhyanathan, van Dijck, Gillespie, or Sweeney), (c) one AI-in-sociology frontier work (Argyle 2023, Hewitt et al., Park-Bernstein, Bender 'Stochastic Parrots' 2021), and (d) one specific risk + one specific opportunity the discipline faces in the next decade.
question.rubric: Mentions: algorithmic society — Zuboff *Surveillance Capitalism* (2019, surveillance capitalism + behavioral surplus + instrumentarian power); Eubanks *Automating Inequality* (2018, digital poorhouse + LA + Indiana + Allegheny); Benjamin *Race After Technology* (2019, New Jim Code + engineered inequity); O'Neil *Weapons of Math Destruction* (2016, opacity + scale + damage). Platform sociology — Vaidhyanathan *Anti-Social Media* (2018, Facebook + democracy); van Dijck *Platform Society* (2018); Gillespie *Custodians of the Internet* (2018, content moderation); Sweeney 2013 Google name discrimination + audit-style CSS. AI frontier — Argyle 2023 'Out of One, Many' silicon samples; Hewitt et al. 2024 LLM-augmented methods; Park + Bernstein 2023 generative agents; Bender + Gebru + McMillan-Major + Mitchell 2021 'Stochastic Parrots'; Gray + Suri *Ghost Work* (2019). Risks: bias laundering, compute concentration, displacement of ethnography, replication challenges, privacy + consent. Opportunities: integrated algorithmic + ethnographic + intersectional sociology; just-transition + abolitionist tech policy; new questions for the classical canon. Concludes that sociology's future is the integration of classical theory + computational tools + intersectional attention + AI critique.
